newsitem.title: USA: Clinton again reaches out to Republicans.
newsitem.headline: Clinton again reaches out to Republicans.

text.p: Preaching his bipartisan sermon for the third time in the five days since the election, President Bill Clinton said on Sunday he wanted to reach out to the Republicans, especially on balancing the budget.

"I intend to reach out to them and to express my appreciation to them for their willingness to work with us," Clinton said in an interview on ABC's "This Week with David Brinkley" program, which was taped on Friday.

"With regard to Congress, if I could do one thing, I would pass a balanced budget that would ... open the doors of college to all Americans, and continue the incremental progress we've made in health care reform," he said.

Clinton, a Democrat, easily won re-election on Tuesday, but voters sent a mixed signal by leaving both houses of Congress in the hands of the Republicans. As a result any major reform will have to be hammered out between the parties.

In a sign that this may be harder than Clinton might like, Republican Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said on Sunday Clinton had been "irresponsible" in portraying the Republican position on the Medicare health care program for the elderly.
"On Medicare, he's been irresponsible, he's misled the people, he's misinformed them," Lott said of Clinton's campaign claims on Medicare. "It's been disingenuous."
"He's going to have to basically admit the problem is there, it's more serious than he has acknowledged, and then we'll work together," Lott said on NBC's "Meet the Press" program.

Among the toughest issues facing Clinton is the reform of so-called entitlement programs like Medicare, health care for the elderly and Medicaid, health care for the poor, and the Social Security retirement program.

Clinton, scheduled to leave on a trip to Hawaii and Asia at the end of the week, made the budget a priority on his schedule, inviting the leaders of Congress to the White House on Tuesday to discuss the matter.

In the five days since the election Clinton has sought at every turn to reach out to the Republicans, making this a theme of his victory speech on election night and letting it be known that he is looking for Republicans to join his Cabinet.

One prominent Republican whose name been mentioned for a top job -- retiring Maine Sen. William Cohen -- on Sunday said he was not interested in becoming the director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).
"It's not an area of high interest for me," Cohen, who served on the Senate Intelligence Committee for a decade, told CNN's "Late Edition" program. "I'm not interested in pursuing that now."
Cohen said he would consider an offer to be secretary of state or defense, saying anyone offered one of those two jobs "would have to consider it."
He also said an administration official contacted him about "a range of positions," although he said the White House had not contacted him directly.
White House officials said Clinton was giving top priority to selecting his Cabinet after no less than six Cabinet members made known that they planned to leave government service.
One administration official said Clinton discussed this on Sunday with Erskine Bowles, the North Carolina investment banker he has named to replace Chief of Staff Leon Panetta.

Separately the Washington Post reported on Sunday that Deputy Chief of Staff Harold Ickes was expected to leave the White House after being passed over to replace Panetta, who is returning to California to consider running for governor.
